name: Precision
description: How exact and consistent your measurements are

content.overview: So we just talked about accuracy—being right. Precision is a different animal: it's about how exact and consistent your measurements are, no matter whether they're correct. A scale reading 65.347 kg is more precise than one reading 65 kg, simply because it gives you more detail. {{viz:diagram-01}}
content.explanation:
Let's go back to that dart analogy, because it nails this idea too. Imagine you throw 3 darts:

- All 3 land clumped together in a tight little cluster—even if that cluster isn't near the bullseye. That's PRECISE.
- Darts scattered randomly all over the board. That's NOT precise.

See the difference? Precision doesn't care where you're aiming—it just cares whether you keep landing in the same spot. {{viz:anim-01}}

Same goes for numbers. A scale showing 65.2347 kg is more precise than one showing 65 kg, purely because it reports more decimal places—more fine-grained detail.

But here's the twist that trips people up: that super-precise scale could still be totally WRONG. Imagine it consistently reads 5 kg too high, every single time. It's precise (always gives the same kind of detailed number) but not accurate (the number's just wrong). {{viz:chart-01}}

So here's the big takeaway: you can absolutely be precise without being accurate. Think of a broken clock that's always exactly 10 minutes fast. Check it a hundred times and it's dead consistent—very precise. But it's also always wrong—totally inaccurate.
keyPoints: Precision = exactness and consistency, not correctness
More decimal places usually means more precision
A scale reading 65.347 kg is more precise than one reading 65 kg
You can absolutely be precise without being accurate—don't confuse the two!
Precision tells you how finely you measure, not whether you're right
content.whyItMatters: A precise measurement tells you something real about your tool—how carefully and consistently it can measure. But precision alone won't save you: if the number's wrong to begin with, being consistent about being wrong doesn't help anyone. You need both accuracy and precision to really trust a measurement.
